intro: Check the stop cards first: each one is a condition where you stop the engine before doing anything else. Then pick the symptom that best matches what you are seeing. Possible causes are not listed in any order, so use what you have seen to decide where to start, and do the checks in the order given.
reminder: This is general guidance only. Engines differ, so follow your engine manufacturer's handbook, and if you are unsure or the fault comes back, ask a qualified marine engineer to look at it.

stopCards.title: Low oil pressure
stopCards.stop: Reduce power and stop the engine as soon as the boat is safe.
stopCards.doNotRestart: Do not restart to see whether the warning clears, even if the oil level looks right.
stopCards.getAssistance: If the cause is not clear and corrected, get a qualified engineer to check the engine.

stopCards.title: Overheating or loss of cooling water
stopCards.stop: Reduce power and stop the engine as soon as the boat is safe.
stopCards.doNotRestart: Do not restart until the cause is corrected and the cooling circuit is ready. Never open a hot pressure cap.
stopCards.getAssistance: If you cannot find and fix the cause once the engine has cooled, get qualified help.

stopCards.title: Water coming into the boat
stopCards.stop: Make the boat safe and start pumping. Find where the water is coming in and close its seacock if you can. If the leak is at the engine, its hoses or the shaft, stop the engine as soon as the boat is safe.
stopCards.doNotRestart: Do not restart until the leak is stopped or under control.
stopCards.getAssistance: If the water is gaining or you cannot find the source, call for assistance early.

stopCards.title: Suspected water in the engine (waterlock)
stopCards.stop: Stop cranking at once if the engine turns a little and stops hard, or you hear water.
stopCards.doNotRestart: Do not crank again: forcing an engine with water in a cylinder can bend internal parts.
stopCards.getAssistance: Get qualified assistance before anyone tries to turn the engine again.

stopCards.title: Fuel spraying or leaking
stopCards.stop: Stop the engine at once and keep hands and face away from any spray. Contain spills and keep flames and sparks away.
stopCards.doNotRestart: Do not restart until the leak has been repaired. High-pressure fuel parts are engineer-only work.
stopCards.getAssistance: If fuel may have been injected into the skin, get emergency medical treatment immediately.

stopCards.title: Smoke or fire in the engine space
stopCards.stop: Stop the engine, shut off the fuel supply if you can reach it safely, and get everyone clear. Follow your boat's fire plan and do not open the engine space wide, because fresh air feeds a fire.
stopCards.doNotRestart: Do not restart until the cause has been found and repaired.
stopCards.getAssistance: If there is a fire, or the boat or crew are in danger, call for help immediately.

stopCards.title: Uncontrolled leak at the shaft seal
stopCards.stop: Stop the engine and shaft as soon as the boat is safe. Never adjust a seal on a turning shaft.
stopCards.doNotRestart: Do not run the engine in gear until the leak is under control.
stopCards.getAssistance: Check the bilge pumps can keep up. If the water is gaining or the seal cannot be secured, call for assistance early.

symptoms.title: Exhaust smoke
symptoms.summary: The colour of the smoke is a useful clue. A puff of smoke on a cold start can be normal; heavy smoke, or smoke that does not clear, is telling you something. Smoke inside the engine space is different: use the stop card.

possibleCauses.title: White smoke on a cold start that clears
possibleCauses.detail: Some fuel does not burn fully until the cylinders warm up, especially in cold weather or if a glow plug is weak. If it clears within a minute or two it is usually nothing to worry about.

possibleCauses.title: Black smoke, mainly under load
possibleCauses.detail: There is more fuel than the air can burn. Possible reasons are a dirty air filter, a blocked air intake, or an engine working too hard because of a fouled hull, a fouled propeller or rope round the shaft. A worn injector can do the same.

possibleCauses.title: White smoke or steam with little water coming out
possibleCauses.detail: If the exhaust is dry or spitting rather than flowing, the cooling water is not getting through and the hot exhaust is turning what little there is into steam. Treat this as overheating.

possibleCauses.title: Blue smoke
possibleCauses.detail: The engine is burning its own lubricating oil. It may have been overfilled, or it may have worn piston rings or valve guides. Long periods of idling with little load make it worse.

possibleCauses.title: White smoke that stays when the engine is warm
possibleCauses.detail: Can be serious: coolant may be getting into a cylinder, for example through a failed head gasket. Look for the coolant level dropping with no visible leak.

checkFirst: Note the colour, and whether the smoke appears on a cold start, at idle or only when you open the throttle.
Check that cooling water is coming out of the exhaust as it normally does. If the flow is weak or missing, go to Overheating.
Check the air filter and make sure nothing is blocking the engine's air intake.
With the engine stopped, check the oil level on the dipstick. An overfilled engine can burn the extra oil and smoke blue.
Think about load: a dirty hull, a fouled propeller or something round the shaft all make the engine work harder.

symptoms.title: Won't start
symptoms.summary: Split the problem in two. Either the engine does not turn over when you press start, or it turns over but does not fire.

possibleCauses.title: Flat or weak battery, or a poor connection
possibleCauses.detail: The starter turns slowly, clicks or does nothing. Loose or corroded terminals give exactly the same symptoms as a flat battery.

possibleCauses.title: A control left in the wrong position, or an engine inhibit
possibleCauses.detail: The stop control not pushed fully home, the gear lever out of neutral, or the battery isolator or key switch off. On an electronically controlled engine, a fault or immobiliser can also prevent starting, usually with a warning on the panel.

possibleCauses.title: Air in the fuel
possibleCauses.detail: Running low on fuel, changing a filter or a loose fuel connection can let air in. The engine turns over normally but will not fire, or fires briefly and dies.

possibleCauses.title: No fuel reaching the engine
possibleCauses.detail: An empty tank, a closed fuel valve or a blocked filter. Water or sludge in the tank can block a filter very quickly.

possibleCauses.title: Not enough heat to light the fuel
possibleCauses.detail: A diesel lights its fuel with the heat of compression. In cold weather it relies on its cold-start aid, usually glow plugs. Failed glow plugs, or not pre-heating for long enough, can stop it firing.

possibleCauses.title: Blocked air intake or low compression
possibleCauses.detail: A blocked intake starves the engine of air. A worn engine with low compression may not get hot enough to fire, which shows most from cold.

possibleCauses.title: Water in the cylinders
possibleCauses.detail: Serious. If the engine turns a little and then stops hard, water may have flooded back from the exhaust after a lot of cranking. Do not crank again; get qualified assistance, because forcing it can bend internal parts.

checkFirst: Gear lever in neutral, stop control pushed fully in, battery isolator and key switch on.
Listen when you press start. Nothing at all, a single click, slow turning and normal turning each point to different causes.
If it turns slowly or just clicks, check the battery and make sure its terminals are clean and tight.

If it turns normally but will not fire, check the stop control is fully home, then that there is fuel in the tank, the fuel valve is open and there is no water in the filter bowl. On a cold day, pre-heat as the handbook describes.

Crank in short bursts with a rest between them, as your handbook advises. If the engine repeatedly cranks but does not start, stop and follow the wet-exhaust warning above; never run the engine with the raw-water seacock closed.

Warning A is shown first, verbatim, with the waterlock stop card, consistent with lesson 8.2. Causes now include an engine inhibit, air intake and compression (S13). Please approve.

symptoms.title: Overheating
symptoms.summary: A high temperature reading, an overheat alarm, steam in the exhaust or a dry exhaust all mean the engine is not being cooled properly.

possibleCauses.title: Blocked raw water intake or strainer
possibleCauses.detail: Weed, a plastic bag or debris over the hull inlet or packed into the strainer stops the cooling water.

possibleCauses.title: Raw water seacock closed
possibleCauses.detail: Often left closed after maintenance, after the boat has been laid up, or after a crew member closed it for safety.

possibleCauses.title: Worn or broken water pump impeller
possibleCauses.detail: The rubber vanes of the raw water pump wear, crack and break off, particularly if the pump has run dry. Broken pieces can lodge further along the system.

possibleCauses.title: Slipping or broken drive belt
possibleCauses.detail: On many engines the belt also drives the fresh water (coolant) pump. A squeal, or a battery that stops charging at the same time, are clues.

possibleCauses.title: Low coolant in the fresh water circuit
possibleCauses.detail: On engines with a closed coolant circuit, a leaking hose, pump seal or cap lets the level fall until the engine overheats.

possibleCauses.title: Stuck thermostat or blocked heat exchanger
possibleCauses.detail: A thermostat that stays closed, or a heat exchanger furred with scale or blocked by impeller pieces, stops heat being carried away.

checkFirst: Before anything else, follow the stop-engine condition above and let the engine cool. Do not open a hot coolant pressure cap or touch hot hoses or exhaust parts.
Think back to the exhaust before you stopped. Little or no water coming out points to the raw water side: intake, seacock, strainer, pump drive or impeller.
Once cool, check the raw water seacock is open. Close it before opening the strainer to clear it, and open it again before the engine runs.
Check the drive belt is in place, undamaged and tight.
On an engine with a coolant circuit, check the level in the header tank.
If all of those are fine, inspect the impeller. If any vanes are missing, find the pieces before you run the engine again.
symptoms.reviewNote: S04: stop-engine condition D is shown first, verbatim, with the overheating stop card; the blocked strainer is no longer called the most common cause, causes are unranked, and every check happens after the engine has cooled. Please approve.

symptoms.title: Stops suddenly
symptoms.summary: An engine that stops by itself is often starved of fuel or air, or stalled by something round the propeller. How it stopped tells you where to look.

possibleCauses.title: Blocked fuel filter
possibleCauses.detail: Rough weather stirs up water, sediment and fuel bug from the bottom of the tank, and it collects in the filters. The engine usually slows and fades over a few seconds.

possibleCauses.title: Out of fuel, or air drawn into the fuel
possibleCauses.detail: A low tank can uncover the pick-up pipe when the boat heels or rolls, letting air in. A loose connection on the suction side does the same.

possibleCauses.title: Rope, net or weed round the propeller
possibleCauses.detail: The engine stalls as soon as it is put in gear, or stops abruptly with a thump. Often there is vibration first. A low idle speed, a gearbox fault or a binding shaft can also stall an engine in gear.

possibleCauses.title: Water in the fuel
possibleCauses.detail: Water does not burn. A slug of it reaching the injectors stops the engine, often after rough weather or refuelling.

possibleCauses.title: Blocked fuel tank vent
possibleCauses.detail: As fuel is used, a vacuum builds in a tank that cannot breathe, until the lift pump can no longer draw fuel. The engine may restart after a rest and then stop again.

possibleCauses.title: Serious mechanical fault
possibleCauses.detail: If the engine stopped hard with an alarm, a bang or a smell of burning, it may have overheated, lost oil pressure or seized. Do not restart it.

checkFirst: Make the boat safe first. You have lost propulsion, so sail, anchor or call for help as the situation needs.

Think about how it stopped. Fading over a few seconds suggests fuel; stopping as you put it in gear suggests the propeller, though idle speed, the gearbox or the shaft are also possible; a hard stop with an alarm or a bang means do not restart.
Check the fuel level and that the fuel valve is open.
Look in the primary filter bowl for water or dirt.
Before checking round the propeller, make sure the engine is stopped and cannot be started. Never go near the propeller with the engine running.

symptoms.title: Low oil pressure
symptoms.summary: The oil pressure warning light comes on, the alarm sounds or the gauge reads low while the engine is running.

possibleCauses.title: Low oil level
possibleCauses.detail: From a leak, from oil being burnt over time, or from the level simply not being checked. Easy to check once the engine has stopped, but a normal level does not rule out a real loss of pressure.

possibleCauses.title: Faulty sender, switch or wiring
possibleCauses.detail: The warning can be false, caused by a failed pressure switch or a loose wire. Treat it as real until you have proved otherwise.

possibleCauses.title: Thin or contaminated oil
possibleCauses.detail: Oil diluted by diesel, the wrong grade of oil, or oil that has been overheated cannot hold its pressure.

possibleCauses.title: Oil filter problem
possibleCauses.detail: A blocked filter, the wrong filter, or a filter fitted badly after an oil change.

possibleCauses.title: Worn oil pump or bearings
possibleCauses.detail: Can happen on older engines. This needs a qualified engineer.

checkFirst: Do not restart to see whether the warning clears.
Wait a few minutes for the oil to drain back to the sump, then check the level on the dipstick with the boat as level as possible.
Look under the engine and around the oil filter for fresh oil.
Look at the oil on the dipstick. If it smells of diesel, looks milky or feels unusually thin, do not run the engine; get advice.
If the oil and filter were changed recently, check that the right filter is fitted, it is tight and its seal is in place.

If the level is right and the oil looks normal, still treat the warning as real: the switch or wiring may be at fault, but only a test gauge proves it. Get a qualified engineer to measure the real pressure before you run the engine again.
symptoms.reviewNote: Audit note 32, safety revise (P0, S03): stop-engine condition C is shown first, verbatim, with the stop card; 'the most common cause' is removed and causes are unranked; the checks begin with 'do not restart'. Please approve, including the advice against running with milky or fuel-smelling oil.

symptoms.title: Not charging
symptoms.summary: The charge warning light stays on with the engine running, or the battery voltage does not rise when the engine is started. Either indicates a charging-system fault, not necessarily a failed alternator.

possibleCauses.title: Loose, slipping or broken drive belt
possibleCauses.detail: The alternator is driven by a belt. A slipping belt often squeals, especially when the engine speeds up or the batteries are low.

possibleCauses.title: Loose or corroded connections
possibleCauses.detail: At the alternator, the battery terminals or the isolator switch. Damp engine spaces make corrosion common.

possibleCauses.title: Isolator or charge switch set wrongly
possibleCauses.detail: Battery switches set to a position that disconnects the battery being charged, or a charge-splitting device that has failed.

possibleCauses.title: Battery that will not hold its charge
possibleCauses.detail: An old or deeply discharged battery may accept little charge, so it looks as if nothing is charging it.

possibleCauses.title: Faulty alternator or regulator
possibleCauses.detail: Once the belt, wiring and battery have been ruled out, the alternator needs testing.

checkFirst: Look at the drive belt. If it has broken and also drives the coolant pump, stop the engine, because it will soon overheat.
With the engine stopped, check the belt's tension and look for cracks, glazing or fraying.
Check the battery terminals and the alternator wiring for loose or corroded connections.
Check the battery isolator and any charge switches are set as they normally are.
If you have a voltmeter, compare the battery voltage with the engine stopped and then running above idle. With no rise, the battery is not being charged.
